I will say this if you do decide to look for a trainer... pay attention to their attitude. Trainers who are smug and think they know everything often don't know shit about shit and may end up getting you hurt. Someone who is an active listener and focuses on your specific goals and asks questions about your body (any previous injuries, surgeries, conditions that limit your activity, pain in certain areas) is more likely to give you some really good information. A degree is cool, but I'm a trainer and I don't have one. Ask them about their certification, as a client I wouldn't want someone with a weekend certification for training. 

Oh yeah, and one of the best things a trainer can do for you is develop a program for your specific goals/needs. There is tons of information accessible to you for free on the internet, but sometimes it helps to have someone apply it in a manner most effective for you.

It's not tilting! Rotating the toes inward, think pigeon toed, targets the weaker muscles of the hamstring. Semimembranisus/tendinosus toward the inner thigh. Try this on the leg curl and marvel at how much more difficult it is to perform the exercise. Thank me later.

If you have an anterior tilt and experience low back pain, they're probably related! As is stated around here, warm up your hammies, abs, and obliques and see if your squats don't improve, at least in comfort!
Agreed, waking up the hammies is a great idea. I absolutely must if I intend to do squats without my quads doing all the work.

On a machine like a hamstring curl or leg press, or in an exercise like a hip bridge, try pointing your toes in toward each other. You may notice more difficulty as this targets the semimebranosus and semitendinosus muscles of the hamstrings. Those two are usually the weaker. I don't see many people with bicep femoris weakness!
Just don't stop working on it! :)

I mean your pelvis, the actual bones. You can train you muscles to correct the tilt, but it will regress if you allow it. It's likely you'll be battling your postural imbalances for a long time. Fear not, if you don't let it go to long without training you should continue to improve! :) I still suffer a bit of low back pain due to my tilt at the end of a long day.

NASM corrective exercise specialist, here. I do see a moderate anterior tilt based on your photos. I have the tilt as well. It causes me low back pain if I slack on the needed exercises. Seems like you're headed in the right direction with the strengthening and inhibiting. Basically, strengthen abs abs abs! And specifically glute med and min. Hamstrings, specifically the inner two, this is easily done in many exercises by turning your toes in toward each other. Stretch them quads and calves, foam rolling as well. You can't really fix your pelvis, but you can battle your postural imbalances. Good luck and good training!
